bib.title: LLM Augmented LLMs: Expanding Capabilities through Composition

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "LLM Augmented LLMs: Expanding Capabilities through Composition" (CALM). Rachit Bansal, Bidisha Samanta, Siddharth Dalmia, Nitish Gupta, Shikhar Vashishth, Sriram Ganapathy, Abhishek Bapna, Prateek Jain, Partha Talukdar (Google Research / Google DeepMind). arXiv:2401.02412v1 [cs.LG], 4 Jan 2024. The PDF text prints no venue. The extraction shows only the arXiv stamp, so "ICLR 2024" is NOT confirmed by this source.

COVERAGE: 58,773 of 58,773 chars read, all 17 pages. That covers the main text, Tables 1-8, appendices A-C and the references (skimmed). Figures 1 and 2 are only partly legible as text. No extraction faults.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: CALM composes a frozen anchor LLM with a frozen smaller augmenting model through learned projections and cross-attention. It adds a few parameters and a small data slice, and it keeps the original capabilities.
  number: about 1.5% added parameters (worked BERT example); 5-7% of the data; the paper's own cost example gives about 2% of mB training cost, or 12% including mA.
  setup: Worked arithmetic with BERT-small/large and assumed 2% data and 10% mA size. It is not measured on PaLM2.
  quote: "Hence, number of parameters added during composition ≈ 1.5% of those in mB." / "since only 5-7% of the total mB fine-tuning data is required to train CALM" / "Cost of training mA + CALM ≈ (0.10 ∗ X + 0.02 ∗ X) = 0.12 × X = 12% of mB training."
  where: Appendix C, pp. 16-17
- claim: Low-resource translation XX to English on FLORES-200. The composed model beats the anchor on most languages and nearly matches continued pre-training.
  number: avg chrF1 46.1 (CALM) vs 41.7 (PaLM2-S) vs 37.2 (mA) vs 48.2 (mB further pre-trained on NTL). CALM beats the anchor on 175 of 192 languages.
  setup: Anchor PaLM2-S, augmenting model PaLM2-XXS pre-trained on NTL (about 1000-language web corpus). 5-shot, 10-language subset shown. CALM trained on about 5% of the NTL data.
  quote: "PaLM2-S (mB) 32.6 24.2 44.6 50.8 50.9 5.4 9.5 69.0 61.0 68.6 41.7 ... CALM (mA⊕B) ... 46.1 ... mB+NTL (mNTLB ) ... 48.2" and "mA⊕B outperforms both the underlying models for 175 of 192 languages"
  where: Table 2, p. 6; Appendix A.1, p. 14
- claim: Grade-school math (GSM8K) in low-resource languages improves with CALM. Further pre-training the anchor on the NTL data hurt it, which the authors read as forgetting.
  number: LRL avg 25.0 (CALM) vs 22.5 (PaLM2-S) vs 22.6 (further pre-trained mB); HRL avg 31.8 vs 28.0 vs 25.6. CALM wins on 18 of 25 LRL and 9 of 10 HRL languages. Silver-translated LRL set: PaLM2-S 18.6, CALM 21.4 on the full 25-language average (Table 6).
  setup: Multilingual GSM8K (Shi et al. 2023) for HRL. LRL set machine-translated by Google Translate into 25 languages. Accuracy.
  quote: "mB when fine-tuned on DNTL leads to worse performance than the pre-trained mB indicating forgetting." / "Gains on the HRL set suggests that CALM avoids catastrophic forgetting."
  where: Table 3, p. 7; Table 6, p. 14
- claim: Code. The composed model improves completion and text-to-code over the anchor. Further pre-training the anchor on code (mCode) collapses code-to-text, which the authors attribute to catastrophic forgetting.
  number: HumanEval P@1 22.5 (CALM) vs 16.4 (mB) vs 19.5 (mA) vs 24.3 (mCode). MBPP 32.2 vs 28.6 vs 28.0 vs 43.0. Python C2T chrF1 30.5 vs 30.4 vs 28.0 vs 18.9. Abstract claims "relative improvement of 40%". The text says 6.1% and 3.6% absolute gains over mB on CC and T2C.
  setup: mA is PaLM2-XXS further pre-trained on open-source GitHub code, mB is PaLM2-S. CALM trained on 7% of the code data. HumanEval zero-shot, MBPP 3-shot, CodeXGlue 3-shot.
  quote: "We observe that fine-tuning mB on DCode leads to a significant decline in the C2T performance due to catastrophic forgetting." and "6.1% and 3.6% absolute gains over mB on the CC and T2C tasks"
  where: Table 4, p. 8
  Note: mCode beats CALM on HumanEval and MBPP, so CALM does not match full further pre-training on code completion. The abstract's "on-par with fully fine-tuned counterparts" is only partly supported by the table. The paper does not state where the 40% comes from.
- claim: Synthetic key-value test. The composed model solves a task neither frozen model can, and it generalises to held-out keys.
  number: KV-Arithmetic 84.3% (CALM) vs 0.7 (mA) vs 0.0 (mB). mA memorises KV at 98.1%.
  setup: 25K string-integer pairs. mA is PaLM2-XXS trained on substitution. mB is PaLM2-XS. Composition trained on examples spanning only 20% of the keys.
  quote: "DKV-MATH 0.7 0.0 84.3" and "CALM generalizes to the entire key-value set despite training with arithmetic examples spanning only 20% of the keys."
  where: Table 1 and Fig. 1, pp. 2, 6
- claim: Ablations show the gain comes from the specialised mA, not from the added parameters. CALM also beats LoRA at equal added parameters.
  number: FLORES chrF1 CALM 60.5 vs vanilla mA 59.2 vs random mA 58.8 vs mA as encoder 59.3 vs LoRA 59.2. Languages beating mB: 175 vs 115 vs 43 vs 102 vs 82. GSM8K LRL 21.4 vs LoRA 20.9. HumanEval 22.5 vs LoRA 18.3. MBPP 32.2 vs 28.7.
  setup: Same added-parameter count. LoRA trained on the same DC data.
  quote: "This finding validates that performance gains seen with CALM is a result of utilizing mA and not the added ΘC parameters."
  where: Table 5, p. 9
  Note: Table 5 row labels are scrambled in the extraction. The column order is mNTL/Code, CALM, vanilla, random, encoder, LoRA.
- claim: Method details. Every 4th layer of mA is used (NA/n = 4). A linear projection maps mA to mB's width. Cross-attention takes mB's layer as the query and the projected mA as key and value. The output is added residually. Decoding is iterative, so both models are re-run on the growing sequence.
  number: none besides NA/n = 4
  setup: PaLM2-XXS (mA), PaLM2-XS or PaLM2-S (mB). Layer-selection formulas are given in section 3.1.
  quote: "HA⊕Bj = HBj + fcross(fproj(HAi), HBj)"
  where: §3.1, p. 4; §4, p. 5
- claim: The paper motivates composition by the skewed share of code and low-resource languages in LLM pre-training corpora. This is an assertion, with no data.
  number: none
  quote: "LLMs have a wealth of world knowledge, they could often lack the specific knowledge of code syntax due to a skewed representation of code data in their pretraining corpora."
  where: §4.3, p. 8

LIMITS
- All experiments use PaLM2 (XXS, XS, S), which is closed. The size and training mix of the models are not stated.
- Only one augmenting model is tested. Multi-augmenter composition is "left for future work".
- The LRL GSM8K set is silver-standard machine translation. Table 7 back-translation overlap ranges from about 55 to 83. The performance delta is 1.15 to 1.70, so small but not zero.
- The qualitative examples in Table 8 are admitted to be cherry-picked.
- The mCode / mNTL baselines are "skylines". The cost comparison in Appendix C is an assumed linear-FLOPs estimate, not a measurement.
- It needs access to weights and intermediate activations of both models, and backprop through the anchor.
- There are no standard-deviation or multi-seed results.
- The paper is about capability composition, not about pre-training objectives or data mixes. Its link to the note on pretraining data is indirect: low-resource and code data are underrepresented in pre-training, and continued pre-training on them causes forgetting. The paper does not measure data-mix ratios.

BUILDS ON
- Alayrac et al. 2022 (Flamingo cross-attention)
- Vaswani et al. 2017 and Raffel et al. 2020 (encoder-decoder cross-attention)
- Hu et al. 2022 (LoRA)
- Houlsby et al. 2019, Pfeiffer et al. 2021 (AdapterFusion), Wang et al. 2021 (K-Adapter)
- Model merging: Wortsman et al. 2022, Ilharco et al. 2022, Matena & Raffel 2022, Yadav et al. 2023, Muqeeth et al. 2023
- Dalmia et al. 2022 (LegoNN)
- Zeng et al. 2022, Shen et al. 2023 and Schick et al. 2023, for models-as-tools
- Data and benchmarks: Caswell et al. 2020 and Bapna et al. 2022 (NTL), Costa-jussà et al. 2022 (FLORES-200), Cobbe et al. 2021 and Shi et al. 2023 (GSM8K), Chen et al. 2021 (HumanEval), Austin et al. 2021 (MBPP), Lu et al. 2021 (CodeXGlue), Google 2023 (PaLM 2)

CODE
- Cross-attention definition (§3.1): "headk = Attn.(QB, KA, VA), QB = HBjWQk , KA, VA = fproj(HAi)WKk , fproj(HAi)WVk" and "HA⊕Bj = HBj + fcross(fproj(HAi), HBj)"
- Parameter count (App. C.1): "# Parameters added during composition = n ∗ (DA ∗ DB + 3 ∗ D2B)"

FIGURES
- Fig. 1 (p. 2): overview of CALM. Frozen mA and mB with cross-attention over every 4th layer. It shows the three uses: key-value, low-resource language and code.
- Fig. 2 (p. 14): per-language gain over the anchor across all 192 FLORES languages, sorted from low to high resource. The gains are largest for the lowest-resource languages and diminish for higher-resource ones. The data is in the plot only, so the numbers were not extracted. I did not run the captions script.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found.
- The venue is not printed in the PDF. Check ICLR 2024 externally before you cite it.
- Table 5 row labels and the Fig. 2 axis text are scrambled in the extraction.
- The abstract says "up to 13%" for low-resource tasks and "40% relative" for code, and I could not trace either to a table. Cite the table numbers instead.
